key_insight: ID-MAE links impairment prediction with reconstructing missing gaze and driving trajectories, allowing the model to learn from more than impairment labels alone.
problem_solved: Ground-truth labels for drivers’ cognitive states are expensive to collect at scale, making it difficult to model how driver state, gaze, and behavior interact.
method: Use a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder to model driver impairment alongside gaze and trajectory data.
Predict the impairment label as a masked token.
Add a self-supervised objective that reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory information.
impact: The approach could help practitioners use multimodal driving data when cognitive-state labels are scarce. The provided abstract is incomplete, so performance gains and experimental conclusions cannot be assessed.
visual_elements: Input icons representing driver gaze, vehicle trajectory, and impairment labels.
A masking diagram showing hidden gaze samples, trajectory segments, and a label token.
An ID-MAE architecture diagram with outputs for impairment prediction and gaze/trajectory reconstruction.
A split-objective graphic contrasting label prediction with self-supervised reconstruction.
paper_title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
paper_authors: John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell
